body.heading: A solved game
paragraphs: Tic-tac-toe is what game theorists call solved: if both players play perfectly, every game ends in a draw. That is not a disappointment — it makes the game a perfect laboratory. When you lose at tic-tac-toe, you made a specific, findable mistake, and you can learn to never make it again.

A few reliable guidelines: the centre is the strongest opening square, because it touches four lines. A corner is next best. If your opponent opens in the centre, answer in a corner — answering on an edge against a centre opening is the classic way to lose.

body.heading: The fork: two threats at once
paragraphs: The winning weapon is the fork: a move that creates two separate lines, each one move from completion. Your opponent can block only one line per turn, so the other completes on your next move. Every tic-tac-toe victory against a decent player is a fork or the threat of one.

Defence is the mirror image: watch for squares where your opponent could create two threats at once, and spoil the fork before it exists — sometimes by making a threat of your own that forces them to defend instead.

body.heading: A strategy to borrow
paragraphs: Here is the practical summary. Open centre or corner. Block any line where your opponent has two. Take any line where you have two. And always glance one move ahead for forks — yours to make, theirs to prevent.

Then teach the fork to someone else and enjoy the brief arms race that follows. Games this small are not really about winning; they are about how quickly a complete understanding can spread around a table.

takeaway: With best play from both sides, tic-tac-toe always ends in a draw — and the fork, two threats at once, is how you punish a mistake.
